papers.abstract: When large language models (LLMs) use in-context learning (ICL) to solve a new task, they must infer latent concepts from demonstration examples. This raises the question of whether and how transformers represent latent structures as part of their computation. Our work experiments with several controlled tasks, studying this question using mechanistic interpretability. First, we show that in transitive reasoning tasks with a latent, discrete concept, the model successfully identifies the latent concept and does step-by-step concept composition. This builds upon prior work that analyzes single-step reasoning. Then, we consider tasks parameterized by a latent numerical concept. We discover low-dimensional subspaces in the model's representation space, where the geometry cleanly reflects the underlying parameterization. Overall, we show that small and large models can indeed disentangle and utilize latent concepts that they learn in-context from a handful of abbreviated demonstrations.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM confidence estimation by analyzing the stability of internal representations under targeted adversarial perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CCPS, a method that estimates LLM confidence by analyzing the stability of internal representations under adversarial perturbations, achieving significant improvements in calibration and discrimination metrics across diverse models and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CCPS provides an efficient, accurate, and generalizable method for LLM confidence estimation, enhancing the trustworthiness of LLMs in critical domains.
papers.key_findings:
CCPS reduces average Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% (up to 88%) and Brier score by 21% (up to 45%) compared to the best baseline.
CCPS increases average Accuracy by 5 percentage points, AUCPR by 4 percentage points, and AUROC by 6 percentage points.
CCPS generalizes across diverse LLM architectures (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) and model scales (8B to 32B parameters).
CCPS performs well on both multiple-choice and open-ended question answering formats.
CCPS is parameter-efficient, adding only around 9.5k trainable parameters, compared to baselines that may add millions.
papers.abstract: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese Smiley, Kundan S Thind, Mohammad M. Ghassemi. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2025.

papers.title: Is Grokking Worthwhile? Functional Analysis and Transferability of Generalization Circuits in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile?
papers.core_contribution: Grokking does not represent genuine acquisition of generalized reasoning; instead, it integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers show limited transferability to novel facts.
papers.conclusion: Grokking merely integrates memorized facts into naturally established circuits, and grokked transformers have limited transferability to novel facts, suggesting a trade-off between data scarcity and computational resources.
papers.key_findings:
Non-grokked and grokked models follow identical reasoning paths on in-distribution compositional queries, indicating that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an established reasoning structure.
Grokking and the formation of a Generalization Circuit are not intrinsically linked; behavioral grokking can occur without circuit formation.
Generalization Circuits exhibit limited transferability; they do not imply full mastery of compositional logic and struggle with new facts in certain positions.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints limit exhaustive exploration of fake grokking due to prolonged training cycles.
Findings are constrained to parameter-sharing Transformer architectures and may not extend to standard transformers.
future_direction: Systematically categorize which data distributions favor circuit formation over pattern memorization.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at factual retrieval, they often struggle with the "curse of two-hop reasoning" in compositional tasks. Recent research suggests that parameter-sharing transformers can bridge this gap by forming a "Generalization Circuit" during a prolonged "grokking" phase. A fundamental question arises: Is a grokked model superior to its non-grokked counterparts on downstream tasks? Furthermore, is the extensive computational cost of waiting for the grokking phase worthwhile? In this work, we conduct a mechanistic study to evaluate the Generalization Circuit's role in knowledge assimilation and transfer. We demonstrate that: (i) The inference paths established by non-grokked and grokked models for in-distribution compositional queries are identical. This suggests that the "Generalization Circuit" does not represent the sudden acquisition of a new reasoning paradigm. Instead, we argue that grokking is the process of integrating memorized atomic facts into an naturally established reasoning path. (ii) Achieving high accuracy on unseen cases after prolonged training and the formation of a certain reasoning path are not bound; they can occur independently under specific data regimes. (iii) Even a mature circuit exhibits limited transferability when integrating new knowledge, suggesting that "grokked" Transformers do not achieve a full mastery of compositional logic.

papers.title: Neuron Empirical Gradient: Discovering and Quantifying Neurons’ Global Linear Controllability
papers.research_question: How do neuron activations influence model outputs? Can shifting neuron activations precisely control output probabilities? Can neuron empirical gradients capture general language skills beyond factual knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a global linear relationship between neuron activations and model outputs, termed neuron empirical gradient (NEG). It proposes NeurGrad, an efficient method to estimate NEG, and demonstrates that NEGs can represent a wide range of language skills through skill neuron probing.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals a linear relationship between neuron activations and model outputs, introduces an efficient method (NeurGrad) to quantify it, and demonstrates that neuron empirical gradients can effectively represent diverse language skills, advancing neuron-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activations and output shifts are linearly correlated within a certain range, quantified as the neuron empirical gradient (NEG).
NeurGrad efficiently estimates NEG, outperforming existing neuron-ranking methods in accuracy and speed.
NEGs can capture general language skills across diverse tasks, as shown through skill neuron probing on the MCEval8K benchmark.
Skill neurons identified via NEGs exhibit properties of efficiency, robustness, flexibility, and interdependency.
The linearity holds for multi-neuron interventions, though predictability decreases with more neurons or larger activation shifts.
papers.limitation: Linearity weakens when more neurons are involved or when activation shifts are larger, reducing predictability.
papers.abstract: While feed-forward neurons in pre-trained language models (PLMs) can encode knowledge, past research targeted a small subset of neurons that heavily influence outputs.This leaves the broader role of neuron activations unclear, limiting progress in areas like knowledge editing.We uncover a global linear relationship between neuron activations and outputs using neuron interventions on a knowledge probing dataset.The gradient of this linear relationship, which we call the neuron empirical gradient (NEG), captures how changes in activations affect predictions.To compute NEG efficiently, we propose NeurGrad, enabling large-scale analysis of neuron behavior in PLMs.We also show that NEG effectively captures language skills across diverse prompts through skill neuron probing.Experiments on MCEval8k, a multi-genre multiple-choice knowledge benchmark, support NEG's ability to represent model knowledge.Further analysis highlights the key properties of NEG-based skill representation: efficiency, robustness, flexibility, and interdependency.The code and data are released.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Analyzing Machine‐Learned Representations: A Natural Language Case Study
papers.research_question: To what extent do machine-learned sentence embeddings encode and utilize abstract, composable relational structure for natural language inference, and how does the training distribution influence the learned representations and heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: This paper uses cognitive science methods to analyze sentence embeddings, revealing that a state-of-the-art model (InferSent) relies on simple, ecologically valid heuristics (overlap, antonyms, negation) rather than abstract compositional rules for NLI, but can learn such rules with targeted training data augmentation, albeit with limitations in generalization (context-tying).
papers.conclusion: Methods from cognitive science and psycholinguistics, such as diagnostic test sets, provide valuable insights into machine-learned representations, revealing heuristic strategies and their origins in training data. While augmentation can encourage learning of abstract rules, limitations like context-tying suggest tabula rasa neural networks may require combinatorially large data or built-in inductive biases to achieve human-like systematicity.
papers.key_findings:
InferSent sentence embeddings perform poorly on a diagnostic test set (Comparisons dataset) requiring abstract relational reasoning, achieving near-chance accuracy.
Analysis of InferSent's errors reveals it uses heuristic strategies (overlap, antonyms, negation) that are ecologically valid in the SNLI training data.
When fine-tuned or trained on an augmented dataset containing examples of the abstract rules, InferSent can achieve near-perfect performance on the diagnostic test and generalize to unseen words (zero-shot reasoning).
However, the learned representations exhibit 'context-tying': generalization is poor for words previously seen only in a different syntactic context, analogous to human belief bias.
The training distribution has a strong effect on the representations learned, and simple heuristics can be learned instead of systematic rules if they explain variance in the training data.
papers.limitation:
The learned representations exhibit 'context-tying', hindering generalization of abstract rules to words seen previously in different contexts.
Achieving fully systematic representations via data augmentation alone may require combinatorially large amounts of training data.
future_direction: Study how systematicity evolves over the course of augmented training and how much augmentation is needed.
Integrate top-down knowledge of language structure with methods that learn to generate adversarial augmentations.
Build useful inductive biases into models to scalably learn systematic representations.
Use diagnostic metrics like context-tying to benchmark systematicity in other domains (e.g., scene understanding, planning).
papers.abstract: As modern deep networks become more complex, and get closer to human-like capabilities in certain domains, the question arises as to how the representations and decision rules they learn compare to the ones in humans. In this work, we study representations of sentences in one such artificial system for natural language processing. We first present a diagnostic test dataset to examine the degree of abstract composable structure represented. Analyzing performance on these diagnostic tests indicates a lack of systematicity in representations and decision rules, and reveals a set of heuristic strategies. We then investigate the effect of training distribution on learning these heuristic strategies, and we study changes in these representations with various augmentations to the training set. Our results reveal parallels to the analogous representations in people. We find that these systems can learn abstract rules and generalize them to new contexts under certain circumstances-similar to human zero-shot reasoning. However, we also note some shortcomings in this generalization behavior-similar to human judgment errors like belief bias. Studying these parallels suggests new ways to understand psychological phenomena in humans as well as informs best strategies for building artificial intelligence with human-like language understanding.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: When Less Language is More: Language-Reasoning Disentanglement Makes LLMs Better Multilingual Reasoners
papers.research_question: Can reasoning and language processing in LLMs be disentangled to improve multilingual reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning and language can be disentangled in LLMs by ablating language-specific components in hidden states, leading to improved multilingual reasoning performance across diverse models and languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that language and reasoning are separable in LLMs, and the proposed training-free intervention provides a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language-reasoning disentanglement via activation ablation consistently improves multilingual reasoning performance across 10 open-weight LLMs and 11 typologically diverse languages.
There is a negative correlation between language-specific activation and reasoning accuracy; removing language-specific signals improves reasoning.
Middle layers are most effective for disentanglement, improving reasoning while preserving language fidelity, whereas upper-layer ablation degrades output fluency.
The training-free intervention achieves comparable or superior results to post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Low-resource languages show a trade-off: reasoning improves with ablation, but language fidelity drops more sharply than in high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
After ablation, models tend to default to English, which may reduce language fidelity, especially for low-resource languages.
The exact ratios of pretraining data for different languages are unknown, which limits a definitive explanation of the convergence phenomenon.
future_direction: Further investigation into the convergence of non-English representations to English after ablation.
Exploring adaptive ablation strategies to balance reasoning improvement and language fluency for low-resource languages.
Combining the training-free intervention with post-training methods for enhanced multilingual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs), with performance disproportionately favoring high-resource languages. Drawing inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human reasoning functions largely independently of language processing, we hypothesize that LLMs similarly encode reasoning and language as separable components that can be disentangled to enhance multilingual reasoning. To evaluate this, we perform a causal intervention by ablating language-specific representations at inference time. Experiments on 10 open-weight LLMs spanning 11 typologically diverse languages show that this language-specific ablation consistently boosts multilingual reasoning performance. Layer-wise analyses further confirm that language and reasoning representations can be effectively disentangled throughout the model, yielding improved multilingual reasoning capabilities, while preserving top-layer language features remains essential for maintaining linguistic fidelity. Compared to post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, our training-free language-reasoning disentanglement achieves comparable or superior results with minimal computational overhead. These findings shed light on the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual reasoning in LLMs and suggest a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.

papers.title: Far from the Shallow: Brain-Predictive Reasoning Embedding through Residual Disentanglement
papers.research_question: How can reasoning-specific components in LLM representations be isolated, and how do these isolated reasoning embeddings align with human brain activity during language comprehension?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a residual disentanglement method to isolate reasoning-specific embeddings from LLM hidden states, and uses these embeddings to provide neural evidence for abstract reasoning computations during language comprehension, showing distinct spatiotemporal brain alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides compelling neural evidence for an abstract reasoning computation during language comprehension and offers a robust framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Residual disentanglement yields four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning.
The isolated reasoning embedding accounts for unique variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and recruits visual regions beyond classical language areas.
The neural signature for reasoning peaks later (~350-400ms) than signals for lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with a processing hierarchy.
Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings are biased toward linguistically shallow features (lexicon, syntax), masking the contributions of deeper cognitive processing like reasoning.
The method provides a framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on ECoG data provides limited spatial coverage, with insufficient sampling in frontal regions crucial for reasoning.
The role of layers beyond the reasoning saturation layer (around layer 30 in Qwen2.5-14B) remains unclear; they may encode more abstract representations.
future_direction: Integrate complementary modalities such as fMRI to improve spatial resolution.
Explore larger models optimized for multi-step reasoning to reveal stronger or more specialized reasoning signals.
Investigate how higher-level representations in deeper layers (beyond reasoning saturation) might align with cortical hierarchies or large-scale cognitive organization.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the human brain progresses from processing simple linguistic inputs to performing high-level reasoning is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. While modern large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to model neural responses to language, their internal representations are highly "entangled," mixing information about lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. This entanglement biases conventional brain encoding analyses toward linguistically shallow features (e.g., lexicon and syntax), making it difficult to isolate the neural substrates of cognitively deeper processes. Here, we introduce a residual disentanglement method that computationally isolates these components. By first probing an LM to identify feature-specific layers, our method iteratively regresses out lower-level representations to produce four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and, critically, reasoning. We used these disentangled embeddings to model intracranial (ECoG) brain recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech. We show that: 1) This isolated reasoning embedding exhibits unique predictive power, accounting for variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and even extending to the recruitment of visual regions beyond classical language areas. 2) The neural signature for reasoning is temporally distinct, peaking later (~350-400ms) than signals related to lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with its position atop a processing hierarchy. 3) Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings can be misleading, as their predictive success is primarily attributable to linguistically shallow features, masking the more subtle contributions of deeper cognitive processing.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: Learning Inductive Biases with Simple Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do simple neural networks develop inductive biases like the shape bias, and under what conditions? How does the acquisition of this bias relate to vocabulary acceleration, mirroring child development?
papers.core_contribution: Simple neural networks can learn a shape bias from very few examples, and the development of this bias predicts vocabulary acceleration in the networks, consistent with developmental processes in children.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can learn inductive biases like the shape bias from limited data, and the dynamics of this learning mirror child development, suggesting a connection between artificial and human learning.
papers.key_findings:
Multilayer perceptrons develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories using abstract bit-vector patterns.
Convolutional neural networks develop a shape bias with as few as 6 examples of 8 object categories using synthetic images.
Networks show greater sensitivity to changes in shape than color after shape bias training, as shown by parametric manipulation of stimuli.
The development of the shape bias in CNNs correlates with the onset of vocabulary acceleration, mirroring the correlation observed in children.
Color bias training requires less data than shape bias training and does not follow the same two-step generalization process.
future_direction: Investigate the hypothesis of initializing large-scale image recognition models with shape bias training using ImageNet-scale DNNs.
papers.abstract: People use rich prior knowledge about the world in order to efficiently learn new concepts. These priors - also known as "inductive biases" - pertain to the space of internal models considered by a learner, and they help the learner make inferences that go beyond the observed data. A recent study found that deep neural networks optimized for object recognition develop the shape bias (Ritter et al., 2017), an inductive bias possessed by children that plays an important role in early word learning. However, these networks use unrealistically large quantities of training data, and the conditions required for these biases to develop are not well understood. Moreover, it is unclear how the learning dynamics of these networks relate to developmental processes in childhood. We investigate the development and influence of the shape bias in neural networks using controlled datasets of abstract patterns and synthetic images, allowing us to systematically vary the quantity and form of the experience provided to the learning algorithms. We find that simple neural networks develop a shape bias after seeing as few as 3 examples of 4 object categories. The development of these biases predicts the onset of vocabulary acceleration in our networks, consistent with the developmental process in children.

papers.title: Unraveling the cognitive patterns of Large Language Models through module communities
papers.research_question: How are cognitive skills organized within Large Language Models (LLMs), and do they exhibit modular specialization similar to biological systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a network-based framework linking cognitive skills, LLM architectures, and datasets, finding that LLMs exhibit a distributed organization of cognitive skills within module communities, contrasting with the localized specialization in biological systems.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that LLMs internalize cognitive skills in a distributed manner across module communities, suggesting that effective fine-tuning strategies should leverage network-wide dependencies and distributed learning dynamics rather than rigid modular interventions.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a community structure in their modules that is associated with cognitive skills, but this structure does not align with predefined cognitive function categories.
Community-based fine-tuning induces the most substantial weight changes but does not yield a clear accuracy advantage over fine-tuning randomly selected modules or all modules.
Cognitive skills in LLMs are distributed across module communities, showing a pattern more akin to weak-localization architectures (e.g., avian brains) than the strong task-specific localization seen in the human brain.
Module communities within LLMs are tightly connected internally but also exhibit cross-community interactions, as measured by network metrics like participation coefficient and Z-score.
The distribution of skills across module communities is statistically independent of predefined cognitive categories, indicating a unique organizational principle in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The abstract cognitive skills defined could be further refined to capture a more nuanced spectrum of human cognition.
Computational constraints influenced model selection, though the methodology is scalable.
The comparable performance between randomly selected modules and community-specific fine-tuning reveals a complex interplay between module specialization and task performance that requires further investigation.
future_direction: Explore network-wide dependencies, inter-layer connectivity, and adaptive optimization strategies that harness the model’s distributed learning potential more effectively.
Investigate the subtleties of modular interactions and the inherent flexibility of LLMs.
Apply the proposed methodology to larger architectures and datasets.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have reshaped our world with significant advancements in science, engineering, and society through applications ranging from scientific discoveries and medical diagnostics to Chatbots. Despite their ubiquity and utility, the underlying mechanisms of LLM remain concealed within billions of parameters and complex structures, making their inner architecture and cognitive processes challenging to comprehend. We address this gap by adopting approaches to understanding emerging cognition in biology and developing a network-based framework that links cognitive skills, LLM architectures, and datasets, ushering in a paradigm shift in foundation model analysis. The skill distribution in the module communities demonstrates that while LLMs do not strictly parallel the focalized specialization observed in specific biological systems, they exhibit unique communities of modules whose emergent skill patterns partially mirror the distributed yet interconnected cognitive organization seen in avian and small mammalian brains. Our numerical results highlight a key divergence from biological systems to LLMs, where skill acquisition benefits substantially from dynamic, cross-regional interactions and neural plasticity. By integrating cognitive science principles with machine learning, our framework provides new insights into LLM interpretability and suggests that effective fine-tuning strategies should leverage distributed learning dynamics rather than rigid modular interventions.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and share representations of morphosyntactic concepts (e.g., grammatical number, gender, tense) across typologically diverse languages?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models develop shared, causally relevant representations of abstract grammatical concepts across many languages, even when trained on imbalanced, English-centric data.
papers.conclusion: Large language models learn robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts, suggesting an internal 'lingua franca' of shared conceptual representations rather than language-specific encodings.
papers.key_findings:
A significant fraction of sparse autoencoder features encoding morphosyntactic concepts are shared across typologically diverse languages.
Ablating multilingual features significantly decreases classifier performance across languages, indicating models rely on shared representations.
Causal interventions on single multilingual features can selectively modify model behavior (e.g., in machine translation) with minimal side effects.
The identified multilingual features are human-interpretable and their sharing patterns are consistent across models with different training data balances (Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B).
The most massively multilingual features (shared across many languages) explain most of the probes' behavior, despite being a small subset.
papers.limitation:
Feature steering interventions require careful tuning of activation scales and can sometimes lead to degenerate or unexpected outputs.
There is a distinction between a model encoding a concept (as measured by probes) and using it during generation; some features causal for probes may not affect generation.
Human interpretation of features is likely biased and may not fully capture the model's internal concept spaces.
Sparse autoencoders may struggle to recover features that are encoded in a non-linear manner.
future_direction: Optimizing feature steering methods to avoid degenerate outputs and improve reliability.
Further investigating the distinction between concept representation and concept generation in models.
Exploring non-linear methods for feature discovery to capture more complex encodings.
papers.abstract: Jannik Brinkmann, Chris Wendler, Christian Bartelt, Aaron Mueller. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Think Like the Brain? Sentence-Level Evidences from Layer-Wise Embeddings and fMRI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the similarity between LLM representations and human brain activity is due to model scaling or deeper alignment with human language processing principles.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that instruction tuning and semantic comprehension ability, rather than model scale alone, drive the alignment between LLM representations and human brain activity during sentence processing.
papers.conclusion: Instruction tuning and semantic comprehension capacity, not merely parameter size, are key drivers of neural similarity, and the alignment is anatomically and functionally specific to intermediate layers and hemispheric specializations.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of LLMs show higher correlation with brain activity than final layers.
Instruction-tuned models exhibit better performance and stronger neural alignment compared to their base versions.
Hemispheric asymmetry in brain regions aligns with functional specialization, with left-hemisphere regions correlating more with core language processing and right-hemisphere regions with higher cognitive functions.
future_direction: Training procedures that explicitly target alignment with brain data to produce more cognitively plausible models.
Developing hybrid neuro-symbolic LLMs to better reflect distributed and lateralized processing patterns observed in the brain.
papers.abstract: Understanding whether large language models (LLMs) and the human brain converge on similar computational principles remains a fundamental and important question in cognitive neuroscience and AI. Do the brain-like patterns observed in LLMs emerge simply from scaling, or do they reflect deeper alignment with the architecture of human language processing? This study focuses on the sentence-level neural mechanisms of language models, systematically investigating how layer-wise representations in LLMs align with the dynamic neural responses during human sentence comprehension. By comparing hierarchical embeddings from 14 publicly available LLMs with fMRI data collected from participants, who were exposed to a naturalistic narrative story, we constructed sentence-level neural prediction models to identify the model layers most significantly correlated with brain region activations. Results show that improvements in model performance drive the evolution of representational architectures toward brain-like hierarchies, particularly achieving stronger functional and anatomical correspondence at higher semantic abstraction levels. These findings advance our understanding of the computational parallels between LLMs and the human brain, highlighting the potential of LLMs as models for human language processing.

papers.title: Can LLMs Detect Their Confabulations? Estimating Reliability in Uncertainty-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How does in-context information influence model behavior and response uncertainty, and can uncertainty signals be used to predict response reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a context-controlled evaluation framework to study how context quality affects LLM responses, shows that token-level uncertainty can misalign with correctness under misleading context, and proposes a probing-based method using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation for improved reliability detection.
papers.conclusion: Providing accurate context improves model accuracy and confidence, while misleading context leads to confidently incorrect outputs, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. The probing-based approach using uncertainty-guided hidden state aggregation improves reliability detection over uncertainty-only baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Correct context improves both answer accuracy and model confidence.
Misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses.
Token-level uncertainty does not always align with correctness, particularly under misleading context.
Probing classifiers using aggregated hidden states from high-uncertainty tokens outperform direct uncertainty metrics for reliability detection.
Aggregating features from multiple tokens yields better performance than single-token features.
future_direction: Developing reliability-aware generation and context validation/filtering mechanisms for multi-turn or retrieval-augmented generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prone to generating fluent but incorrect content, known as confabulation, which poses increasing risks in multi-turn or agentic applications where outputs may be reused as context. In this work, we investigate how in-context information influences model behavior and whether LLMs can identify their unreliable responses. We propose a reliability estimation that leverages token-level uncertainty to guide the aggregation of internal model representations. Specifically, we compute aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty from output logits to identify salient tokens and aggregate their hidden states into compact representations for response-level reliability prediction. Through controlled experiments on open QA benchmarks, we find that correct in-context information improves both answer accuracy and model confidence, while misleading context often induces confidently incorrect responses, revealing a misalignment between uncertainty and correctness. Our probing-based method captures these shifts in model behavior and improves the detection of unreliable outputs across multiple open-source LLMs. These results underscore the limitations of direct uncertainty signals and highlight the potential of uncertainty-guided probing for reliability-aware generation.

papers.title: The Mechanics of Conceptual Interpretation in GPT Models: Interpretative Insights
papers.research_question: What are the observable representation patterns that characterise conceptual interpretation within language models? Can we localise specialised representational patterns to derive an interpretation model within language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces concept editing, a variation of knowledge editing, to uncover conceptualization mechanisms in LLMs, and through analysis of MLP, MHA, and hidden states, reveals distinct patterns of semantic processing.
papers.conclusion: The work elucidates how transformer models process semantic information through distinct component interactions, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
MLP layers employ key-value retrieval and context-dependent processing, focusing on specific lexical and semantic features.
MHA layers show distributed nature with higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration.
Hidden states emphasize the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process, indicating gradual information building.
Concept interpretation involves a collaborative process among model components, with compositionality being critical.
Patterns are consistent across languages (English and Spanish) and across alternative definitions, indicating robust processing strategies.
papers.abstract: Locating and editing knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their accuracy, safety, and inference rationale. We introduce ``concept editing'', an innovative variation of knowledge editing that uncovers conceptualisation mechanisms within these models. Using the reverse dictionary task, inference tracing, and input abstraction, we analyse the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Multi-Head Attention (MHA), and hidden state components of transformer models. Our results reveal distinct patterns: MLP layers employ key-value retrieval mechanism and context-dependent processing, which are highly associated with relative input tokens. MHA layers demonstrate a distributed nature with significant higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration. Hidden states emphasise the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process. We observe evidence of gradual information building and distributed representation. These observations elucidate how transformer models process semantic information, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques. Our work highlights the complex, layered nature of semantic processing in LLMs and the challenges of isolating and modifying specific concepts within these models.

papers.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive elements of reasoning manifest in LLMs, and how do they differ from human reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements for reasoning and conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of human and LLM reasoning traces, revealing that LLMs underutilize cognitive elements correlated with success and that test-time reasoning guidance can improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reasoning failures and enables principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms, while models possess latent capabilities that can be elicited with structural guidance.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs underutilize cognitive elements that are correlated with success, especially on ill-structured problems.
Humans use more abstraction and conceptual processing, while LLMs rely on surface-level enumeration.
Test-time reasoning guidance that scaffolds successful cognitive structures improves performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
The research community focuses on easily quantifiable cognitive elements (like sequential organization) and neglects meta-cognitive controls (like self-awareness).
Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously.
papers.limitation:
Human participants are educated adults; comparison with children might yield different insights.
Models are tested on a limited set of problem types.
future_direction: Using the taxonomy for training and evaluation of LLMs
Developing cognitive architectures based on the taxonomy
Extending the analysis to more problem types and models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning & knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and conduct the first large-scale empirical analysis of 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, complemented by 54 human think-aloud traces, which we make publicly available. We find that models under-utilize cognitive elements correlated with success, narrowing to rigid sequential processing on ill-structured problems where diverse representations and meta-cognitive monitoring are critical. Human traces show more abstraction and conceptual processing, while models default to surface-level enumeration. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements (sequential organization: 55%, decomposition: 60%) but neglecting meta-cognitive controls (self-awareness: 16%) that correlate with success. Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffold successful structures, improving performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Are Pretrained Language Models Symbolic Reasoners over Knowledge?
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models learn factual knowledge? Specifically, can they perform symbolic reasoning to infer unseen facts, and what factors affect memorization of facts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that PLMs can learn some one-hop symbolic reasoning rules but overgeneralize, struggle with two-hop reasoning, and that memorization is influenced by frequency and schema conformity.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that BERT can to some extent infer facts not explicitly seen during training via symbolic rules, and effective knowledge acquisition combines memorization and symbolic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can learn one-hop rules like equivalence and implication, but overgeneralizes symmetry and inversion.
BERT struggles with two-hop reasoning (composition) unless provided with richer semantic context (schema).
BERT does not learn a general concept of negation; it relies on co-occurrences.
Memorization is successful for frequent facts and schema-conformant facts; exceptions are harder to memorize unless repeated.
When memory capacity is limited, schema-conformant facts and exceptions compete based on frequency.
papers.limitation:
Variation in generated data is more limited than in naturally occurring data.
Semantics are deliberately restricted to one rule only per generated corpus.
We do not investigate effects of model and corpus size.
future_direction: Relax the simplifying assumptions made in the study.
Improve PLMs' ability to learn symbolic rules by imposing additional inductive biases on architectures or modifying training corpora.
papers.abstract: How can pretrained language models (PLMs) learn factual knowledge from the training set? We investigate the two most important mechanisms: reasoning and memorization. Prior work has attempted to quantify the number of facts PLMs learn, but we present, using synthetic data, the first study that investigates the causal relation between facts present in training and facts learned by the PLM. For reasoning, we show that PLMs seem to learn to apply some symbolic reasoning rules correctly but struggle with others, including two-hop reasoning. Further analysis suggests that even the application of learned reasoning rules is flawed. For memorization, we identify schema conformity (facts systematically supported by other facts) and frequency as key factors for its success.

papers.title: Can the Inference Logic of Large Language Models be Disentangled into Symbolic Concepts?
papers.research_question: Whether large language models encode sparse symbolic concepts and if these concepts can be used to explain inference scores and prediction errors.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the inference score of large language models can be disentangled into a small number of sparse symbolic concepts, which are transferable and can explain prediction errors.
papers.conclusion: The paper has empirically verified that LLMs encode sparse symbolic concepts with high transferability and discrimination power, and these concepts can explain prediction errors.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse symbolic concepts can accurately estimate LLM inference scores on all masked input sentences.
Symbolic concepts encoded by LLMs exhibit high transferability across similar sentences.
Disentangled symbolic concepts can identify exact reasons for LLM prediction errors.
The distribution of interaction effects shows that only a few concepts have salient effects, confirming sparsity.
Concepts extracted are consistent with human cognition and factual knowledge.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we explain the inference logic of large language models (LLMs) as a set of symbolic concepts. Many recent studies have discovered that traditional DNNs usually encode sparse symbolic concepts. However, because an LLM has much more parameters than traditional DNNs, whether the LLM also encodes sparse symbolic concepts is still an open problem. Therefore, in this paper, we propose to disentangle the inference score of LLMs for dialogue tasks into a small number of symbolic concepts. We verify that we can use those sparse concepts to well estimate all inference scores of the LLM on all arbitrarily masking states of the input sentence. We also evaluate the transferability of concepts encoded by an LLM and verify that symbolic concepts usually exhibit high transferability across similar input sentences. More crucially, those symbolic concepts can be used to explain the exact reasons accountable for the LLM's prediction errors.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: The Neural Race Reduction: Dynamics of Abstraction in Gated Networks
papers.research_question: How does network architecture (specifically pathways of information flow) affect learning dynamics, representation learning, and generalization in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Gated Deep Linear Network framework and shows that learning dynamics exhibit a neural race bias towards shared representations, enabling systematic generalization and multi-task transfer.
papers.conclusion: The GDLN framework reveals how architecture controls information flow and learning dynamics, leading to a bias towards shared representations that enables systematic generalization and multi-task learning.
papers.key_findings:
The GDLN framework allows exact reduction of learning dynamics to singular value dynamics.
Learning dynamics in structured networks can be conceptualized as a neural race, with faster learning for pathways that share more structure.
There is an implicit bias towards shared representations, which facilitates zero-shot generalization to untrained input-output pathways.
The dynamics from small random weights converge to the maximally shared solution, as validated on naturalistic datasets.
The degree of sharing required for generalization depends on the fraction of trained pathways, with around 40% sufficient for strong generalization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not provide a mechanism to select the gating structure; it is assumed to be given.
The theoretical analysis assumes diagonalizable dataset statistics and linear networks with gating, though validation is done with relaxed assumptions.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for inferring the optimal architecture and gating for a given setup.
papers.abstract: Our theoretical understanding of deep learning has not kept pace with its empirical success. While network architecture is known to be critical, we do not yet understand its effect on learned representations and network behavior, or how this architecture should reflect task structure.In this work, we begin to address this gap by introducing the Gated Deep Linear Network framework that schematizes how pathways of information flow impact learning dynamics within an architecture. Crucially, because of the gating, these networks can compute nonlinear functions of their input. We derive an exact reduction and, for certain cases, exact solutions to the dynamics of learning. Our analysis demonstrates that the learning dynamics in structured networks can be conceptualized as a neural race with an implicit bias towards shared representations, which then govern the model's ability to systematically generalize, multi-task, and transfer. We validate our key insights on naturalistic datasets and with relaxed assumptions. Taken together, our work gives rise to general hypotheses relating neural architecture to learning and provides a mathematical approach towards understanding the design of more complex architectures and the role of modularity and compositionality in solving real-world problems. The code and results are available at https://www.saxelab.org/gated-dln .

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Investigating task-specific prompts and sparse autoencoders for activation monitoring
papers.research_question: How do prompted probing and SAE-based probing compare for activation monitoring in language models, and under what constraints (e.g., data availability, compute) are they most effective?
papers.core_contribution: Prompted probing is a data-efficient and effective method for activation monitoring, especially in low-data regimes. SAE-based probing can be effective when inference-time compute is limited, but prompted probing is recommended when inference-time compute is available.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends prompted probing when inference-time compute is available due to its data efficiency and generalization. If inference-time compute is limited, SAE-based probing is a good alternative. Straightforward activation probing is reasonable when both inference-time and train-time compute are limited.
papers.key_findings:
Prompted last token probing is the most data-efficient technique and performs well in low-data regimes.
Prompting is important: prompted last token probe outperforms naive last token probe, especially in low-data regimes.
In high-data regimes, all probing techniques (prompted probing, SAE probing, raw last token probing) can outperform zero-shot model output.
SAE max-pooled probing generalizes poorly out-of-distribution compared to prompted probing in some cases.
For sentiment classification, last token probes perform best, and max-pooling across tokens degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The work does not compare the methods to fine-tuning the model, which is often the method of choice when labeled training data is available.
Estimates of zero-shot monitoring performance are likely pessimistic due to lack of prompt engineering and not using reasoning models or chain-of-thought.
Few-shot prompting did not improve performance in the studied settings, possibly due to context length limitations or the model's inability to extract useful signal.
future_direction: Exploring unsupervised approaches like LAT Scans for monitoring when labeled data is unavailable.
Investigating the mechanisms underlying prompted probing and whether prompted and un-prompted probing rely on shared representations.
More research into model organisms of emergent deceptive monitors to understand collusion risks.
papers.abstract: Language models can behave in unexpected and unsafe ways, and so it is valuable to monitor their outputs. Internal activations of language models encode additional information that could be useful for this. The baseline approach for activation monitoring is some variation of linear probing on a particular layer: starting from a labeled dataset, train a logistic regression classifier on that layer's activations. Recent work has proposed several approaches which may improve on naive linear probing, by leveraging additional computation. One class of techniques, which we call "prompted probing," leverages test time computation to improve monitoring by (1) prompting the model with a description of the monitoring task, and (2) applying a learned linear probe to resulting activations. Another class of techniques uses computation at train time: training sparse autoencoders offline to identify an interpretable basis for the activations, and e.g. max-pooling activations across tokens using that basis before applying a linear probe. However, one can also prompt the model with a description of the monitoring task and use its output directly. We develop and test novel refinements of these methods and compare them against each other. We find asking the model zero-shot is a reasonable baseline when inference-time compute is not limited; however, activation probing methods can substantially outperform this baseline given sufficient training data.
